author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A 1959 novel in which a man who makes his living winning a newspaper puzzle contest slowly discovers his cozy 1950s town is an elaborate fake built to exploit his precognitive talent—Dick's most perfect statement of reality revealed as a construction only after the reader has lived inside it.
page_summary:
Ragle Gumm lives an ordinary life in a small American town, supporting himself by repeatedly winning a newspaper contest called 'Where Will the Little Green Man Be Next?' Then the world starts to crack: a soft-drink stand vanishes and leaves behind a slip of paper reading SOFT-DRINK STAND, a magazine references people who shouldn't exist, small details refuse to cohere. The accumulating wrongness resolves into a revelation—the year is not 1959, the town is a manufactured stage set, and the contest is a disguised instrument for harvesting Gumm's precognition to predict enemy missile strikes in a war he has been shielded from knowing about.

The novel is Dick's classic demonstration that reality is attacked not by dramatic reversal but by the accumulation of small wrong details, so that the reader shares the protagonist's slow slide from unease into vertigo. The scrupulously ordinary suburban surface makes the eventual disclosure more sinister, and the book poses the disturbing ethical question that recurs throughout his work: what is your action worth, and whom are you responsible to, once you learn your entire world is false?

One of Dick's finest early novels, Time Out of Joint anticipates decades of screen fiction about constructed realities. In the Exegesis, PKD returned to it as the earliest fossil of his 1974 experience—reading Gumm's fake world as an unwitting first report of his own conviction that our world conceals its true temporal locus.
